summary:
ORION: OUTPOST COMMAND

Project Summary — NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

ORION: OUTPOST COMMAND is an interactive educational space-exploration simulator that allows students to experience the challenges of establishing and maintaining a human outpost on the Moon or Mars.

The project puts users in command of a space outpost, where they must make important engineering decisions to keep their crew safe and their settlement operational. Players manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, electricity, and food while responding to simulated emergencies and environmental challenges.

Users can explore a solar system map, choose between lunar and Martian missions, upgrade their outpost infrastructure, and learn about real aerospace concepts such as life-support systems, radiation protection, energy storage, greenhouses, and in-situ resource utilization (ISRU).

An ORION mission advisor provides guidance based on the outpost’s current conditions, helping players understand the consequences of their decisions.

Our Mission

Our goal is to make space engineering more accessible and engaging for younger generations by transforming complex scientific and engineering challenges into an interactive learning experience.

What makes ORION different?

Rather than simply teaching students about space exploration, ORION allows them to experience the responsibility of planning and managing a settlement beyond Earth.

details:
ORION: OUTPOST COMMAND 🚀

What is my project?

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to run a base on the Moon or Mars? That’s exactly what inspired me to create ORION: OUTPOST COMMAND.

ORION is an interactive space-outpost simulator that puts users in charge of their own settlement beyond Earth. Instead of just reading about space exploration, users get to experience some of the challenges astronauts and engineers might face when living on another world.

How does it work?

First, users choose their destination: the Moon or Mars. Once they arrive, they become responsible for keeping their outpost running.

They must:

  • Keep track of oxygen, water, power and food.
  • Maintain important outpost systems.
  • Upgrade batteries, greenhouses and water-recycling systems.
  • Deal with simulated challenges like dust storms and radiation alerts.
  • Make decisions that can help or affect the mission.

There’s also ORION, a mission advisor that gives users helpful recommendations based on what’s happening at their outpost.

Every decision matters, because keeping an outpost running isn’t as easy as it looks!

Why did I create it?

I wanted to make learning about space more exciting and interactive. Space exploration isn’t just about rockets and astronauts; it’s also about solving problems, managing limited resources and finding ways to survive in environments very different from Earth.

Through ORION, I hope to encourage students to become more interested in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), while showing them some of the real challenges behind future space missions.

What did I use to build it?

I developed the website using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Wix for hosting and deployment. I also used Canva to create the project presentation.

The simulator uses programmed rules and simplified educational values to represent resource management and mission events. It is a software-based project and does not require specialised physical hardware.

What makes it creative?

My favourite part of this project is that users don’t just learn about space exploration — they get to take part in it.

I combined a solar system theme, an interactive outpost dashboard, resource management, engineering upgrades and unexpected mission events into one experience.

Users can also compare the Moon and Mars and discover how different environments create different challenges.

What did I consider while developing it?

Since I developed this project on my own, I had to think about the design, functionality and educational experience together.

I considered:

  • Scientific relevance and accuracy.
  • The differences between the Moon and Mars.
  • How to make the simulator easy and enjoyable to use.
  • How to explain complicated space concepts simply.
  • How to make the experience educational without making it feel like a normal lesson.

The simulator uses simplified values for learning purposes, not real engineering specifications.

My vision

I believe the future of space exploration is not only about reaching other planets. It’s about figuring out how we can live there.

With ORION, I wanted to give people a small taste of that responsibility and let them think like the engineers, scientists and explorers of tomorrow.

The question isn’t just whether humans can reach the Moon or Mars. It’s whether we can build a place to call home.
